title: How Fernwood cleared a 900-ticket backlog in nine days
description: A nine-person support team went into December with nine hundred unanswered emails. They came out of it answering in seconds.
imageAlt: A painterly meadow of teal and seafoam brushstrokes
quote: Reply cleared the overnight queue in the first week. Mornings start at zero now, and nobody on my team has said the word 'backlog' since.
content:
Fernwood sells furniture that takes eight weeks to build, which means most of their support volume is one question asked a thousand different ways: where is it.

By the first week of December the queue had reached nine hundred. Nine people were answering, and the honest arithmetic said they would still be behind in February. “We were not failing at anything difficult,” says Maya Ellis, who runs support. “We were failing at repeating ourselves.”

The first week

They connected the shared inbox on a Monday and pointed Reply at their help centre and four years of closed tickets. No flows, no decision trees, no labelling exercise. By Wednesday it was answering delivery questions with the real build stage pulled off the order, and by Friday it had taken four hundred conversations off the queue.

The part Maya did not expect was the tone. “It writes like whoever wrote our shipping page, because that is what it read. Our customers did not notice a handover, which is the whole point.”

The first morning I opened the inbox and there was nothing in it, I assumed something had broken.Maya Ellis, Head of Support

What stayed human

Fernwood set the confidence threshold high on anything touching a refund or a damaged delivery. Those still go to a person — but they arrive summarised, with the order open and photographs already attached.

“The handover is the underrated feature,” Maya says. “My team used to spend the first two minutes of every ticket reading. Now they spend it deciding.”

Nine days later

The backlog hit zero on a Wednesday. Fernwood went through their busiest quarter on record without adding a seasonal hire, and first response time settled at eleven seconds against a four-hour target nobody had ever hit.

Two of the nine agents have since moved onto the onboarding team. “That is the number I care about,” Maya says. “Not the deflection rate. The two people who got a better job out of it.”

title: Halcyon doubled its volume and kept its voice
description: The thing Halcyon was most afraid of automating was the way they sound. So they tested that first.
imageAlt: Close-up painterly cream and blush cosmos petals
quote: I was the sceptic. Ten minutes into the trial it answered a returns question better than our own macro, citing the policy page I wrote.
content:
Halcyon has spent six years building a support voice that people screenshot and post. Warm, specific, faintly funny. It is genuinely part of the brand, and it was the reason they had said no to automation three times.

“Every tool we tried sounded like a terms-of-service page,” says Tobias Renn. “We would rather be slow than sound like that.”

The test they actually ran

Instead of a pilot on easy tickets, Halcyon ran Reply against a hundred conversations they had already answered, then had three people guess which replies were theirs. “We got it right about half the time, which is the same as guessing. That was the moment.”

The reason is unglamorous: Reply learned from the replies Halcyon had already written, not from a style guide. The jokes it makes are jokes someone on the team made first.

It is not imitating us. It is quoting us back, in the right place, at three in the morning.Tobias Renn, CX Lead

Doubling without hiring

A collaboration in April doubled inbound volume in a fortnight. Support headcount did not change. Sixty-one per cent of conversations now close without an agent, and CSAT on those sits a tenth of a point above the human average — which Tobias attributes entirely to speed.

What they watch

Halcyon reviews a sample of automated replies every Friday, twenty minutes, two people. “It is a habit, not a rescue operation. We have changed the tone guidance twice in four months.”

The gap report gets more attention. “It tells us which questions our documentation cannot answer. We have rewritten nine help pages because Reply kept flagging them, and every one of those was a real hole.”

title: Northbank's support team stopped working weekends
description: A regulated product, a strict security review, and a rota nobody wanted to be on. All three survived the change.
imageAlt: Painterly sage grasses bending in the wind
quote: It reads like us. That was the thing I was most afraid of losing and the thing it got right first.
content:
Northbank is a payments company, which means two things: the questions are urgent, and the answers are regulated. For four years someone had been on a weekend rota nobody volunteered for.

“The Saturday shift was two hours of real work spread across eight hours of waiting,” says Ines Okonkwo. “It was a terrible use of a Saturday and a terrible use of a person.”

Security first, for once

Northbank's review took five weeks and started before the trial. Field-level redaction for card data, EU data residency, SSO through their existing provider, and an audit log their compliance team could read without asking anyone.

“We have killed tools at this stage before,” Ines says. “This one came with the SOC 2 report and a straight answer about training data. That is rarer than it should be.”

The threshold that made it work

The unlock was per-queue confidence. Anything touching a balance, a dispute, or an account freeze requires near-certainty before Reply answers alone; everything else — card arrival, statement questions, app troubleshooting — is permissive.

We did not have to choose between careful and fast. We got to be careful where it matters and fast everywhere else.Ines Okonkwo, Support Manager

The rota

Weekend coverage came off the rota in March. Reply handles Saturday and Sunday inbound, and a single on-call phone covers the handful of conversations it escalates — down from eleven a day to about three.

“Retention on the support team is the highest it has ever been,” Ines says. “I would like to tell you that is a sophisticated management achievement. It is mostly that people have their weekends.”
